question.text: In the early years of a Cat I/II AIF, the fund NAV typically shows a 'J curve' pattern — that is, the NAV:

answer.text: Rises steadily from Year 1 in a straight line
Initially declines (possibly to negative zones) before climbing as the fund matures
Remains exactly flat until the first exit
Follows the Nifty 50 closely in the first 3 years

explanation.text: The Logic: Per PDF Section 11.9.1: 'In the early stages of a fund, the fund NAV would DECLINE to NEGATIVE zones and as the fund progresses and reaches its maturity years, the NAV tends to CLIMB.' The initial decline reflects setup costs, management fees, and unrealised early-stage valuations not yet appreciating. The Trap: Straight-line rise ignores early drag from fees; flat until first exit is factually wrong (fees bite immediately); Nifty correlation is a listed-market concept inappropriate for private equity. The J-curve is a PE/VC industry norm. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-A and XIX-C test the J-curve. PE/VC industry reports (Bain, Preqin) always reference it. CFA L3 private markets chapter covers it extensively. Manager's Pro-Tip: Set LP expectations about J-curve at fundraising. Show historical J-curve patterns of comparable funds (often provided by GPs anonymously). First-time LPs panic at Year 2 NAV < capital called — pre-emptive education prevents redemption pressure and governance disputes.
